extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and scholars interested in philosophy, ethics, and the evolution of moral ideas (readers of Popular Science Monthly)
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical essay sketching seven developmental 'stages' by which conscience arises and matures under evolutionary and social influences; mixes natural-history, legal, and religious illustrations to explain moral emergence. Useful as a conceptual taxonomy of moral development rather than an empirical protocol.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Animal Stage
rubrics_metrics.description: The germ of conscience exists in animal life: instinctive contrasts between external destructive force and internal will-to-live produce actions (flight, defense, appeals) that are the raw materials out of which conscience is constructed; animals can be taught to feel 'ought'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that elements of moral feeling (e.g., self-preservation, fear, anticipation, exertion, ecstasy of deliverance) are observable in animals and form the rough 'stones' of conscience; cautions against anthropomorphism but argues for continuity from animal instincts to human conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Intermediate Stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Ape-like man has a vivid sense of his own right to exist but no conception of others' rights — an inheritance of near-perfect selfishness; the nascent conscience acquires an imperative 'must' tied to self-preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterizes early human moral impressions as vague 'thoughts' that become convictions through experience; highlights the emergence of instantaneous, imperative feelings of obligation (doing something because 'I must') prior to social relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Family Stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Maternal care of offspring induces transfer of rights to those loved: early humans learned to extend to others (children) some of the rights they claimed for themselves, though initially as part of the parents' own interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes complexity (polygamy/polyandry) and limits the claim: early care meant seeing children's rights as part of one's own, not as independent claims; sees this stage as the bridge from self-love to benevolence and a foundation for social life, with legal survivals (e.g., Roman paterfamilias) and negative survivals (slaveholder justifications).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Social Stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of likeness among persons allows formation of social relations: primitive idea of others' right to exist emerges and utility (what makes for community survival and welfare) governs concessions/abandonments of rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that the 'golden ethics' (do unto others) becomes both moral rule and scientific fact enabling neighborhood; conscience pays intuitive deference to reciprocal rights (if you have no right to kill me, I have no right to kill you); tracks how conscience helps transfer intuitive deference to changing notions of rightness in society.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Political Stage
rubrics_metrics.description: External law and sanctions (punishment, criminal law) assert community prohibitions (e.g., 'Thou shalt not kill'), and as law appeals to an existing sense of right/wrong the pleasurable sense of duty arises — obedience becomes welcomed when law interprets conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes mere coercion (fear of punishment) from internalized duty (joyful acquiescence in self-sacrifice). Law, custom, and tradition supply sanctions that strengthen conscience and help explain the pleasurable element in duty; warns that law alone cannot create the sense of duty without resonance in conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Ideal or Moral Stage
rubrics_metrics.description: With capacity for abstract thought men form universal moral ideas: rights are generalized to society and nature (everything has its own right), producing ideals (e.g., sanctity of human life) that make individuals 'a law unto themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains movement from utility-based notions to absolute ideals; shows how ideals allow individuals to judge and sometimes disobey authority (refuse to kill even when commanded) and introduces risks (conscience being reified as a special faculty leading to egoistic exaggerations). Connects ideal formation to criticisms and survivals from earlier stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Religious Stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion, especially monotheism, later identifies moral will with the divine will: belief in a single Almighty God integrates righteousness with God's will and can rescue conscience from pure egoism by appealing to an external moral authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Places religious morality late in development; among savages religion often lacks morality, but where belief in one God arises (Hebrew tradition) the voice of tribal opinion becomes the voice of God, providing solemnity and responsibility; notes modern theology's tendency to ascribe supernatural origin to conscience and contrasts scriptural silence on some claims.
